title: Pentagon, Raytheon Sign Up to $6.3 Billion Multi-Year Deal for SM-3 IB Missiles
summary: The Pentagon and Raytheon have signed a multi-year contract worth up to $6.3 billion for SM-3 Block IB interceptors, months after a framework deal to raise production.
content:
Raytheon has won a multi-year Pentagon contract worth up to $6.3 billion to build and sustain Standard Missile-3 Block IB interceptors, the Navy's principal defense against short- and intermediate-range ballistic missiles.

The Missile Defense Agency awarded the deal on Oct. 7, and Raytheon announced it the following day. Listed in the Pentagon's daily awards digest under contract number HQ0851-27-C-E001, it runs for five years with options for two more. The base value is $4.43 billion; if the options are exercised, the ceiling rises to about $6.34 billion.

The award is structured as an undefinitized contract action, a mechanism that lets work begin immediately while final terms are negotiated. The government obligated $454.2 million in fiscal 2026 procurement funds at signing — a fraction of the ceiling, and not the amount Raytheon will ultimately be paid. Work is centered on Raytheon's missile facilities in Tucson, Arizona, and Huntsville, Alabama, and is expected to run through Oct. 31, 2034.

## Replenishing combat-tested stocks

The contract's purpose is straightforward: rebuild the interceptor inventories the United States has spent in real fighting. The SM-3 was used in combat for the first time in 2024, fired by Navy destroyers defending Israel against Iranian ballistic missile barrages. Those engagements proved the weapon — and emptied magazines the Pentagon is now racing to refill.

"This award underscores Raytheon's commitment to increasing production of critical munitions," Raytheon President Phil Jasper said, describing the Block IB as combat-proven and central to keeping fleets and allies defended.

Under Secretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment Michael P. Duffey said the missile had "proven its operational superiority against any adversary," adding that the contract "provides production certainty to our defense industrial base, breaks sub-tier manufacturing bottlenecks, and ensures that our fleets and combatant commands have the interceptors required."

## What the missile does

The SM-3 Block IB is a midcourse interceptor. Launched from Aegis-equipped destroyers and cruisers — or from the Aegis Ashore sites in Europe — it climbs above the atmosphere, releases a kinetic kill vehicle, and destroys incoming ballistic missiles by sheer collision, carrying no explosive warhead of its own. The Block IB added an improved infrared seeker and better steering than earlier variants, sharpening its ability to pick real warheads out from decoys.

## Why multi-year matters

Demand for missile defense has climbed on nearly every front. Beyond the Middle East engagements, the war in Ukraine has shown what sustained missile and drone campaigns do to air-defense stocks, and U.S. planners are blunt that American magazines were sized for shorter wars. Multi-year contracts are the Pentagon's preferred answer: steady, predictable orders that let industry invest in tooling and suppliers with confidence rather than surging and stalling on single-year buys.

## A munitions buying spree

The award is the latest in a run of outsized Pentagon munitions deals. In October, Raytheon secured a contract worth up to $24.4 billion for Standard Missile-6 interceptors; in July, Lockheed Martin won a $58.6 billion Patriot missile contract. Together they reflect the administration's push to expand weapons production and lock contractors into long-term manufacturing commitments.

Raytheon says it has already been investing in expanded Standard Missile capacity. But industry executives have warned that congressional funding remains the binding constraint: without appropriated dollars, even signed contract ceilings cannot become production lines. For now, the SM-3 line in Tucson has its orders — and the Navy has one less magazine to ration.

title: Boeing Wins F/A-XX Contract for Navy's Next-Generation Stealth Fighter
summary: Boeing has won the F/A-XX contract to build the Navy's next-generation carrier-based stealth fighter, one of the most anticipated awards in years.
content:
Boeing has won the Navy's F/A-XX contract, the award for the service's sixth-generation carrier fighter, in a decision announced Sept. 29 that hands the company both of the Pentagon's next-generation fighter programs.

The contract covers the full-scale development phase and is valued at more than $20 billion, including multiple test aircraft for ground, airworthiness, systems, and weapons integration testing. Boeing beat Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman. Northrop has requested a formal debriefing with Navy officials — the customary step before any protest.

## Why Boeing won

According to people familiar with the competition, Boeing prevailed on the strength of years of investment, decades of experience building carrier-based jets, and a design approach that matched the Pentagon's demand for fighters that are easier to upgrade across long service lives. The Pentagon required all three competitors to use common design standards so later modifications could be made quickly as technology evolves.

Boeing also leaned hard on digital design tools, letting engineers, military officials, and maintainers test changes virtually before committing to hardware — a pitch that resonated after the industry's recent struggles with cost overruns on fixed-price development programs.

"Now all of a sudden, it controls the next half century and beyond of US tactical aircraft," Richard Aboulafia of AeroDynamic Advisory said of Boeing. "There's nothing like that in history."

## Two sixth-generation programs, one builder

The F/A-XX award follows Boeing's March 2025 win of the Air Force's F-47, the manned fighter at the heart of Next Generation Air Dominance. With both programs, Boeing now holds the entire American sixth-generation fighter roadmap — a position Lockheed Martin held in the fifth generation with the F-22 and F-35.

"It's an honour to be selected to produce the Navy's first sixth-generation platform," Steve Parker, chief executive of Boeing Defense, Space & Security, said. "Delivering two advanced fighters in parallel was always our plan, and we invested accordingly."

The fighter will be built in St. Louis, Missouri, where construction continues on a secure manufacturing facility tied to an all-digital design and production system.

## What F/A-XX is for

The Navy describes F/A-XX as a sixth-generation strike fighter built around open mission systems architecture, advanced sensors, and greater operational reach — designed to fly farther, carry more, and operate alongside uncrewed collaborative combat aircraft. It is intended to begin augmenting, and ultimately replace, the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet and EA-18G Growler, whose airframes are approaching structural and survivability limits against modern air defenses.

On the same day as the award, the Navy issued Boeing a contract to begin planning the shutdown of Super Hornet and Growler production — a signal of how the service intends to hand the St. Louis workforce and tooling from one generation to the next without a capability gap.

## The road ahead

Technical and programmatic details remain classified under national security rules. The program had at times looked vulnerable, with officials openly questioning whether the industrial base could handle two advanced fighters — plus Northrop Grumman's B-21 bomber — simultaneously. Awarding both fighters to one company may ease that strain through shared knowledge and economies of scale, though it concentrates enormous risk in a single contractor whose defense division has absorbed billions in losses on fixed-price programs.

First-flight timelines and production quantities have not been disclosed. The losing bidders' next moves — and the contract's finer print — should surface in the coming weeks.

title: Taiwan's First F-16 Block 70 Fighters Finally Arrive
summary: Taiwan has taken delivery of its first two new F-16 Block 70 fighters, kicking off a long-awaited fleet expansion as pressure from mainland China grows.
content:
Taiwan's first two F-16 Block 70 fighters touched down at Chihhang Air Base on Oct. 2, ending a wait of nearly seven years and opening the long-delayed renewal of the island's fighter fleet.

The single-seat F-16Cs, serials 6727 and 6728, landed near Taitung on the island's southeast coast at about midday, escorted for the final stretch by Taiwanese F-16s and T-BE-5 Brave Eagle trainers flying in formation. They are the first of 66 Block 70 aircraft Taiwan ordered from the United States in 2019 under an approximately $8 billion deal known locally as the Peace Phoenix Soaring project.

## A long road from Greenville

The jets left Lockheed Martin's F-16 plant in Greenville, South Carolina, on Aug. 17, routing through Fort Worth, Hawaii, and Guam with support from a U.S. Air Force KC-135 tanker. They then sat in Hawaii for more than six weeks — held up first by weather, then by unspecified technical issues, and finally by a U.S.-imposed pause over the optics of a late-September meeting between President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

In a break with past practice, the aircraft had their U.S. Air Force markings removed before leaving Hawaii, revealing the Republic of China Air Force roundel underneath. On previous F-16 deliveries in the 1990s and 2000s, Taiwan's markings were kept covered until the jets arrived home, a nod to political sensitivities that this time was set aside.

The first Taiwanese Block 70 had been unveiled in Greenville in March 2025. Getting from rollout to delivery took another 18 months of testing and calibration to integrate Taiwan-specific systems, wiring, and software — on top of earlier supply-chain disruptions that had already pushed the program years behind its original schedule.

## Why it matters

Taiwan's fighter fleet is among the oldest in the region, and its pilots fly near-daily sorties shadowing Chinese military aircraft operating around the island. The tempo has worn airframes down, and the Block 70s bring relief: Northrop Grumman's AN/APG-83 active electronically scanned array radar, L3Harris's Viper Shield electronic warfare suite, conformal fuel tanks, and General Electric F110 engines put Taiwanese Vipers close to fifth-generation standards in sensing and networking, with compatibility for weapons including the AIM-120D, AGM-88, and Harpoon.

When all 66 arrive, Taiwan will operate more than 200 F-16Vs, counting the 139 older F-16A/Bs upgraded to a similar standard under a program completed in 2023. The new jets will equip the 7th Tactical Fighter Wing, stood up in December 2023, as Chihhang shifts from a training base to a frontline combat station.

## Beijing objects, Taipei presses on

China's Foreign Ministry restated its opposition to U.S. arms sales to Taiwan, with spokesman Guo Jiakun calling the position "consistent and clear." President Lai Ching-te, posting on social media, called the delivery an important milestone for air defense and said investments that raise the cost of any invasion help deter miscalculation.

Defense Minister Wellington Koo told lawmakers that additional jets would arrive before the end of the year, with more than 60 aircraft on the U.S. production line — some already at the delivery stage. After years in which the program became a test of whether approved arms sales could turn into real capability, the two Vipers on the ramp at Chihhang are the first tangible answer.

title: USAF's New HACM Hypersonic Cruise Missile Makes First Release Over Australian Range
summary: The U.S. Air Force has carried out the first release of its Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile over an Australian test range, a milestone after major program delays.
content:
The U.S. Air Force has carried out the first flight-test release of its Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile over an Australian range, moving a long-delayed weapon into the air at last.

The War Zone first reported the test on Oct. 5. An Air Force spokesperson confirmed it the next day, saying the flight took place over "a designated Australian test range" and gathered "crucial data to advance the program's objectives." The spokesperson declined to give a date, describe the launch aircraft, or discuss speed and duration. Open-source reporting widely places the test at the Woomera range in South Australia's desert, the West's favored proving ground for hypersonic flight.

## A U.S.-Australian program

The test was conducted under the Southern Cross Integrated Flight Research Experiment, or SCIFiRE — a U.S.-Australian collaboration the spokesperson described as built on more than 15 years of partnership. Australia's vast, empty ranges offer the long flight corridors hypersonic weapons need, and Canberra is a full partner in the weapon: in Australian service it would be the country's first hypersonic missile and its fastest weapon, with planned carriage on the F/A-18F Super Hornet, EA-18G Growler, F-35A, and P-8A.

RTX's Raytheon is the prime contractor for the munition, with Northrop Grumman building the scramjet engine. The Air Force formally established the HACM program in 2022 after a 2020 industry solicitation. Its roots run deeper: the design draws on DARPA's Hypersonic Air-breathing Weapon Concept and, further back, the Boeing X-51 Waverider flights. The weapon has reportedly been designated AHM-4A under a new joint nomenclature series for missiles.

## How it works

HACM is an air-breathing hypersonic cruise missile. A conventional rocket booster accelerates it to high speed and altitude, then falls away; a scramjet engine takes over, sustaining flight above Mach 5 — more than 3,300 miles per hour — while the missile maneuvers inside the atmosphere. That combination, extreme speed plus the ability to change course in flight, is what makes hypersonic cruise missiles so difficult for air defenses built to track predictable ballistic arcs.

Unlike larger boost-glide weapons, HACM is sized to be carried by tactical fighters as well as bombers, which would let the Air Force hold defended targets at risk from many more platforms. Exact performance figures remain classified.

## Delays and the 2027 target

HACM has suffered significant delays — early plans aimed for flight testing years ago — and the Air Force has taken the unusual step of scaling back the overall test program to protect the schedule. The stated goal now is to be ready for a decision on rapid acquisition in 2027.

That urgency reflects the wider race: China and Russia have fielded hypersonic weapons while the United States has none in operational service. HACM is one of two hypersonic programs the Air Force is pursuing, alongside the larger AGM-183 air-launched rapid response weapon.

The spokesperson would say only that the recent test was "part of our continuous work to advance long-range strike capabilities." For a program that has lived mostly in renderings and budget documents, a real release over a real range is the milestone that counts.

title: Anduril and U.S. Navy Announce $6.6 Billion Push to Expand Submarine Industrial Base
summary: Anduril Industries and the U.S. Navy are investing a combined $6.6 billion to expand America's submarine industrial base, anchored by a new software-defined shipyard.
content:
Anduril Industries and the U.S. Navy have unveiled a $6.6 billion plan to expand America's submarine industrial base, anchored by a giant new manufacturing complex at Sparrows Point, Maryland.

The announcement came Oct. 6 at Tradepoint Atlantic, the former Bethlehem Steel site on Baltimore's waterfront, with President Donald Trump and Maryland Gov. Wes Moore on hand. Anduril will invest $3.7 billion of private capital to build Arsenal-2, a software-defined shipyard of more than two million square feet on a 187-acre site. The Navy has awarded the company a contract worth up to $2.9 billion, with payments tied to demonstrated production results rather than paid upfront — a structure the company says puts most of the execution risk on Anduril, not the taxpayer.

## Components, not whole submarines

Arsenal-2 will manufacture complex components and large assemblies for the Virginia-class attack submarine — items such as torpedo tubes and hull sections — and deliver them to General Dynamics Electric Boat and HII's Newport News Shipbuilding for final assembly. It will not build complete boats. The idea is to add a parallel source for the hardest-to-make parts, letting more construction proceed at once across the industrial base.

The planned facility includes high-bay assembly halls, fabrication areas, reconfigurable production lines, and a 1,200-foot graving dock, with road, rail, and waterfront connections for moving outsized assemblies. It will run on ArsenalOS, Anduril's manufacturing software, coordinating fabrication, assembly, material movement, inspections, and documentation. Permitting and site preparation are beginning now; initial operations are planned for 2030.

The project is expected to create 3,100 direct jobs and more than 11,000 indirect positions, generating about $2 billion in annual economic output.

## Why submarines can't wait

U.S. submarine production has been the Navy's pacing problem for years. The service wants to build two Virginia-class boats a year while simultaneously constructing the Columbia-class ballistic missile submarine — a workload the current base of two nuclear-certified yards and their suppliers has struggled to carry, with skilled labor scarce and lead times stretching.

On top of domestic demand sit the AUKUS commitments: Australia is to receive three, and possibly five, Virginia-class submarines starting in 2032. Meeting that pledge without shortchanging the U.S. fleet requires substantial growth in suppliers, infrastructure, and workforce — exactly the gap Arsenal-2 is meant to fill.

"Submarines are our oceans' apex predators," Vice Adm. Robert Gaucher, who oversees Navy submarine construction, said at the announcement — adding that they are needed "now more than ever" for deterrence, while acknowledging the country's shortfall in shipbuilding capacity.

## An unusual deal structure

In a surprise flourish, Trump said American taxpayers would receive a 40 percent stake in the new shipyard — held through a new Anduril subsidiary created to operate the facility, not as equity in Anduril itself. Further details were not immediately available.

"Today, we're officially launching the construction of the largest new shipyard in the United States," Trump said. "Since World War II, there's been nothing like what we're doing today."

For Anduril — a company built on drones, software, and autonomous systems — the move into heavy manufacturing is a leap. The bet is that tech-industry production methods can succeed where traditional shipbuilding has strained. If Arsenal-2 delivers, it could reshape how America builds undersea weapons. If it stumbles, the submarine programs counting on its parts will feel it first.

title: Navy Orders 30 Drone Ships in Big Push for Medium Uncrewed Vessels
summary: The U.S. Navy has ordered 30 medium uncrewed surface vessels, a major step toward fielding larger drone ship fleets after years of struggle.
content:
The U.S. Navy has ordered 30 medium uncrewed surface vessels from three Louisiana shipbuilders, the service's biggest commitment yet to putting drone ships to sea in numbers.

The announcement came Sept. 29 under the Medium Unmanned Surface Vessel Family of Systems program. Galliano Marine Services, Huntington Ingalls Industries, and Saronic Technologies each received production agreements for 10 vessels, using Other Transaction Authority — a contracting route built for speed rather than the Pentagon's traditional years-long process.

## The money and the timeline

Each agreement covers 10 vessels at an average procurement cost of $40 million per hull, which works out to roughly $1.2 billion for the 30-ship run. Production begins immediately at yards in Loreauville, Houma, and Franklin, Louisiana, with the first deliveries due before the end of fiscal year 2027.

Seven companies competed after completing Phase I at-sea testing. The losers — Sea Machines, Leidos, PacMar Technologies, and Birdon — did not get production deals, though three of them received $15 million each for completing the trials and will be listed on the Defense Department's drone marketplace, keeping them eligible for future work.

## What the Navy asked for

The MUSV marketplace solicitation, issued in March to replace the earlier Modular Attack Surface Craft effort, called for vessels able to cover 2,500 nautical miles at 25 knots while carrying 25 tons on the payload deck. In Phase I, the Navy tested whether the contenders could sense their maritime surroundings, sail without operator assistance, and stay deployed for extended periods.

Saronic will build its 180-foot Marauder design; HII offered Romulus. Galliano Marine Services, which does business as Edison Chouest, has not publicly detailed its entrant.

"Each agreement is for the procurement of 10 MUSV at an average procurement cost of $40 million per vessel," Chris Miller, the Navy's acting portfolio manager for robotic and autonomous systems, told reporters. He called the awards "a significant step forward in translating the strategic vision into a tangible fleet capability."

Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao framed the move as the service's priority to modernize the fleet quickly with autonomous systems.

## Why "medium" matters

Medium USVs sit in the sweet spot the Navy has chased for a decade: big enough to carry meaningful sensors and weapons across ocean distances, small and cheap enough to buy in numbers and risk in contested waters. They are central to the "hybrid fleet" vision — a relatively small number of large manned warships multiplied by scores of robotic ones doing surveillance, mine warfare, electronic warfare, and strike.

Past efforts foundered on reliability, autonomy shortfalls, and shifting requirements. The Navy's plan now is to grow the uncrewed surface fleet from four hulls to 30 by 2030, focused on the Indo-Pacific. Whether these 30 boats become an operational capability or another experiment with hull numbers will depend on what the at-sea testing actually proved — results the Navy has not published in detail.

The choice of Other Transaction Authority is itself a statement of intent. OTA agreements let the Pentagon prototype and buy without the years-long Federal Acquisition Regulation process, and the Navy has used them deliberately here to compress the timeline from competition to hulls in the water. The losing bidders' exclusion from standard protest rights under OTA is part of that trade-off: speed in exchange for the usual legal recourse, a bargain the Navy has decided is worth making as it races to field uncrewed mass in the Pacific.

title: Sweden Launches First Patriot Air Defense Mission to Poland
summary: Sweden has launched its first Patriot air defense mission to Poland as part of a NATO operation, amid a heated domestic security debate.
content:
Sweden will deploy a Patriot air defense unit to Poland in December, the first time Stockholm has sent the U.S.-made missile system on a NATO mission.

The government announced the decision Oct. 6. About 100 personnel from the Air Defence Regiment, supported by the Blekinge Air Wing, will operate the system — known in Swedish service as Luftvärnssystem 103 — under NATO command as part of the alliance's Integrated Air and Missile Defence.

## Guarding the Ukraine lifeline

The unit's task is to protect the NATO logistics hub at Rzeszów in southeastern Poland, the key node through which Western military and civilian aid flows into Ukraine under NATO Security Assistance and Training for Ukraine. The vast majority of military donations for Ukraine transit through Poland, and NATO has reported the hub handling on the order of 18,000 tonnes of materiel a month.

In an era of long-range precision weapons, a rear-area logistics hub is a frontline target. Sweden's deployment puts a scarce, high-end defensive asset over the infrastructure that keeps Ukraine supplied — and over NATO's own ability to move forces across the eastern flank.

"As Allies, we share responsibility for protecting and defending NATO territory," said the Chief of the Swedish Army, Johan Pekkari. "By deploying advanced capabilities from the Air Defence Regiment and Blekinge Air Wing, Sweden will strengthen NATO's eastern flank in Poland while helping to protect the vital support effort for Ukraine."

"The security environment and the complexity of the mission place significant demands on the unit," said Sofia Westermark, commander of the Air Defence Regiment. "We are well trained, well prepared and have the right composition to accomplish the mission."

## Timeline and politics

The mission is set to run from early December through the end of 2026, with preparations underway for a possible extension into the first half of 2027 — an extension that would require the Riksdag's consent, Defense Minister Pål Jonson has noted.

Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said the deployment safeguards the flow of support to Ukraine while strengthening the alliance's eastern flank. It follows a separate Swedish contribution announced days earlier: Gripen fighters began flying NATO missions over Poland on Oct. 1, supporting air defense over the same logistics corridor.

The deployment lands in a charged domestic moment. Sweden joined NATO only recently, and the question of how far Swedish forces should deploy in collective defense remains contested in Stockholm — making the decision to send one of the country's most capable air defense systems abroad as much a political statement as a military one.

Patriot, built by Raytheon, is the alliance's standard for intercepting ballistic and cruise missiles and aircraft. For Poland, already hosting a growing web of allied air defenses, the Swedish battery adds another layer. For Sweden, it marks the step from new ally to burden-sharing contributor — putting hardware, not just signatures, behind its NATO commitments.

The deployment also underscores how seriously NATO now takes the air threat to its rear areas. Russian long-range strikes have repeatedly targeted Ukrainian logistics, and allied air defenses in Poland have been kept on high alert as Russian aircraft and missiles operate near the alliance's borders. Positioning a Patriot battery over Rzeszow is a recognition that in a modern missile war, there is no safe rear — only defended ones.
imageAlt: Sweden Launches First Patriot Air Defense Mission to Poland

title: Pentagon, Lockheed Weigh Multi-Year F-35 Production and Sustainment Deal
summary: The Pentagon and Lockheed Martin are negotiating a multi-year F-35 production and sustainment agreement, though doubts remain over long-term cost savings.
content:
The Pentagon and Lockheed Martin are discussing a sweeping multi-year agreement for the F-35 that could span up to a decade and cover both building the jets and keeping them flying — a deal potentially worth tens of billions of dollars.

The talks were first reported by Breaking Defense on Oct. 9. The idea is not new: officials have weighed multi-year F-35 procurement for years. But the current push, driven by the administration's enthusiasm for long-term weapons agreements, would go further than past efforts by bundling production with sustainment — the maintenance, spares, and support that have long been the program's costliest headache.

## What a decade-long deal would include

"There's been talk about a 10-year, multi-year buy that would include the production as well as sustainment," Matt Milas, president of Honeywell Aerospace's defense division, told Breaking Defense in September. Honeywell is a major F-35 supplier.

A central element would be bulk purchases of spare parts, with the increased flow of components expected to begin around the jet's 21st production lot, roughly three years out. Flooding the supply chain with spares is seen as the most direct lever for lifting the fleet's readiness rates, which have long trailed the Pentagon's targets.

## The skeptics

Not everyone is convinced the structure fits. A person familiar with the negotiations, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed the talks but questioned their premise: multi-year procurement "makes sense where the department has seen success with munitions contracts. It makes less sense for aircraft lot buys" — particularly while elements of F-35 modernization are still in development. "The complexities of sustainment present multiple unique challenges," the person added, doubting Lockheed could demonstrate genuine long-term savings.

The skepticism has history behind it. The F-35's sustainment bill — the cost of operating and maintaining the fleet over its lifetime — has been the program's most stubborn problem for a decade, with per-flight-hour costs resisting years of reduction campaigns. With more than 1,000 jets delivered worldwide, even small shifts in sustainment costs move tens of billions of dollars.

## The backdrop

The talks come days after the Pentagon finalized its deal for F-35 Lots 18 and 19: 296 aircraft for $24.3 billion, an average of $82.4 million per airframe, with deliveries starting this year. Lot 20 is expected to be negotiated as a multi-year contract now that the program is in full-rate production, and Lockheed chief executive Jim Taiclet has said the company can sustain production at 156 jets a year on the strength of U.S. and allied demand.

The Pentagon also continues to spend heavily on the support tail: a recent $1.6 billion spare-parts award was described as the largest in the program's history, and the Navy added $871 million to Lockheed's site-activation contract for standing up new F-35 operating locations.

No timeline for an agreement has been announced. Whether the two sides can bridge the gap between the Pentagon's appetite for long-term savings and industry's caution about locking in sustainment costs will determine whether the decade-long deal becomes the template for the fighter's future — or another idea that stalls in negotiation.

title: GDLS to Deliver New PERCH 2.0 Loitering Munition Prototypes to Army This Month
summary: General Dynamics Land Systems will deliver four PERCH 2.0 loitering munition prototypes to the Army's 1st Cavalry Division by the end of October.
content:
General Dynamics Land Systems will deliver four prototypes of its PERCH 2.0 loitering munition system to the Army by the end of October, putting a new tank-launched drone capability into soldiers' hands within weeks.

The prototypes are headed to the 1st Brigade, 1st Cavalry Division at Fort Hood, where troops will integrate them onto Abrams tanks for experimentation, Scott Taylor, GDLS's director of U.S. growth, told Breaking Defense. The upgraded system is set for its formal debut at the AUSA exposition in Washington this month.

## What PERCH is

PERCH — Precision Effects & Reconnaissance, Canister-Housed — is a modular kit that bolts onto M1A2 Abrams SEPv3 tanks and Stryker vehicles and lets crews launch AeroVironment Switchblade 300 loitering munitions without opening their hatches. The munitions serve as both scouts and strike weapons: loitering over the battlefield to find targets beyond the line of sight, then diving onto them.

The 2.0 iteration reflects direct Army feedback on the first version, which GDLS debuted at last year's AUSA. Soldiers asked for better beyond-line-of-sight capability, easier reloads, and more onboard storage — addressed in part by switching from the larger Switchblade 600 to the smaller Switchblade 300 — plus the ability to fire while fully buttoned up, preserving the vehicle's armor and chemical-biological protection.

The system was refined after a December 2025 demonstration at the Machine Assisted Rugged Sapper event at Fort Hood, where the launcher was tested on Abrams tanks in realistic mission scenarios.

## Built for Ukraine's lessons

GDLS developed the original PERCH with its own research funding, Taylor said, in direct response to the war in Ukraine, feedback from U.S. commanders in Europe, and discussions with III Armored Corps leadership. Loitering munitions have become one of the war's defining weapons, used by the thousands against armor, artillery, and air defenses.

The goal is to give armored brigades their own organic drone-strike capability — the ability to see and hit targets beyond ridgelines and buildings — rather than waiting on assets controlled at higher echelons. In GDLS's concept, the tank becomes a node in a sensor-to-shooter network, launching expendable eyes that can turn into precision weapons when a target appears.

## An urgent Army market

The Army has been moving quickly to push one-way attack drones down to brigade level and below, and several companies are competing for a role. GDLS's advantage is incumbency: it builds the Abrams and the Stryker, and PERCH is designed as a bolt-on kit requiring no permanent changes to the vehicle — a replacement of the turret's rear sponson box and mounting on existing hardpoints.

The company has not disclosed the system's range, warhead details, or expected unit cost. What happens at Fort Hood over the coming months — how soldiers actually use the prototypes, what breaks, what gets requested — will shape whether PERCH 2.0 moves from experiment to a program of record. For now, the prototypes are built, the brigade is waiting, and the clock is ticking toward the end-of-October delivery.

The munition at the heart of the system, AeroVironment's Switchblade 300, is a tube-launched loitering weapon already in U.S. service, small enough to be carried in numbers and precise enough for targets that do not justify larger fires. Pairing it with armor gives tank crews something they have never organically had: their own aerial reconnaissance that can become a strike asset in seconds, without calling up the chain of command.

title: Australia Receives Second HIMARS Tranche Two Years Ahead of Schedule
summary: The Australian Army has received a second tranche of U.S.-built HIMARS rocket launchers, arriving two years ahead of schedule.
content:
Australia has taken delivery of a second tranche of U.S.-built HIMARS rocket launchers — two years ahead of schedule and just a year after the first.

The announcement came Oct. 7 from the Defence Minister. The launchers go to the Army's long-range fires regiment in Adelaide, part of the 10th Fires Brigade, significantly expanding a capability Canberra considers central to its military reorientation toward the Indo-Pacific.

## Ahead of schedule, twice over

Early delivery has become something of a theme for Australia's strike programs. The country fired a Precision Strike Missile from a HIMARS during Exercise Talisman Sabre 2025 — two years ahead of schedule — and earlier this year successfully test-fired the first Australian-manufactured Guided Multiple Launch Rocket System missile from one of its own launchers.

"These highly mobile systems are an incredibly important platform and the delivery of these additional units represents a significant leap in capability for the Australian Army," Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said.

## The 90-launcher plan

The second tranche feeds a much larger ambition. In April, the government announced additional investment in HIMARS and Precision Strike Missiles to stand up a second long-range fires regiment. At full strength, Australia plans to operate up to 90 HIMARS across two regiments within the 10th Fires Brigade.

The ranges are growing too. PrSM gives the force the ability to strike targets up to 500 kilometers away; future increments are expected to push beyond 1,000 kilometers — a reach that would let land-based launchers hold distant maritime and land targets at risk across Australia's northern approaches.

## Building missiles at home

Canberra is pairing the imported launchers with a sovereign munitions effort. Australia and the United States established a cooperative PrSM program last year, and missile production is already underway at a new facility in South Australia, with a second factory due to open near Newcastle, New South Wales, next year.

The investments sit inside the 2026 National Defence Strategy and Integrated Investment Program: up to $37 billion for long-range strike capabilities, and up to $36 billion over the decade for the Guided Weapons and Explosive Ordnance Enterprise.

## Why HIMARS

The truck-mounted system earned its reputation in Ukraine, where precision rockets destroyed Russian ammunition depots and command posts far behind the front lines. For Australia, the appeal is the same: mobile, hard-to-find launchers able to deliver precise long-range fires — and, increasingly, Australian-made rockets to feed them.

The first Australian HIMARS were displayed publicly at the Avalon airshow in 2025. With the second tranche now in country two years early, the program has become a rare bright spot in a procurement landscape more often defined by delay — and a signal of the priority Washington places on arming allies in the region.

The program's pace stands out against its own original plan. The first tranche began with two launchers shown publicly at the Avalon airshow in 2025, and the delivery schedule at the time called for six more by mid-April, another 12 during 2026, and the remaining 22 before the end of 2028. The second tranche arriving two years early suggests both production and the U.S.-Australian coordination behind it are running well ahead of expectations.

title: Could Germany Join GCAP? UK Seeks to Advance Potential Fighter Switch
summary: Britain is pushing to advance talks on Germany potentially joining the GCAP sixth-generation fighter program after the collapse of FCAS.
content:
Britain is pressing ahead with talks that could bring Germany into the Global Combat Air Programme, the sixth-generation fighter it is developing with Italy and Japan, after the collapse of the rival Franco-German FCAS project left Berlin hunting for a new path to a future fighter.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham raised the idea directly with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz during his first visit to Berlin on Oct. 8. "I've indicated to the Chancellor ... our openness to Germany joining GCAP," Burnham told reporters at the German Chancellery. "That is something that we seek to progress in the coming period, working with our other partners, Italy and Japan."

## Exploratory contacts, not negotiations

The contacts are at an early stage. Politico reported on Oct. 4, citing British and German officials and internal German government documents, that the discussions were initiated by London and cover potential cooperation including industrial workshare and Germany's military capability requirements.

Germany's defense ministry has confirmed only "initial coordination talks" on sixth-generation requirements. Aerospace press reports say the two countries' defense ministers have been tasked with examining potential cooperation, but Berlin stresses that no decision — not even a preliminary commitment — has been made.

## Why Berlin is hesitating

Internal German assessments are skeptical. According to Politico, three objections recur: GCAP is shaped by the maritime requirements of island nations — Britain and Japan — rather than the continental air campaign Germany plans for; winning a fair industrial share in a program whose structure is already settled would be difficult; and the documents reference negative experiences with BAE Systems during the Eurofighter Typhoon program.

Berlin is also studying a different route — a partnership with Sweden and Spain that the internal papers reportedly favor. After FCAS collapsed, eight German companies formed "Team Gen 6" to keep sovereign combat-aircraft expertise alive while the government decides which partnership to pursue.

## The FCAS wreckage

The Future Combat Air System formally ended in June 2026 after nine years of deadlock between Dassault Aviation and Airbus Defence and Space over design authority, workshare and intellectual property, with Dassault reportedly demanding up to 80 percent of the fighter work. Only the program's combat-cloud networking element survived the breakup.

The collapse left the German Air Force without a jointly funded successor to the Eurofighter Typhoon — and left GCAP, targeting service entry around 2035, as the only funded sixth-generation fighter program outside the United States with its industrial structure already in place.

## What London wants from Berlin

For Britain, German participation would share costs at a time of budget strain and validate GCAP as Europe's answer after FCAS. Italy has previously said it is open to new members to help share costs; Japan may need convincing. GCAP has already grown once: Canada signed on as an observer in July, a possible path to deeper engagement, and Saudi Arabia has long been named as a potential partner.

But industry executives warn that new partners can bring delays, and one British defense figure noted that GCAP's timeline is fixed — anyone joining now boards a program whose seats and workshare are largely allocated. For Berlin, the question is whether a seat on that train is better than building a new one with Stockholm and Madrid.

title: Arizona Desert Drone Tests Offer Hard Lessons for CENTCOM's Counter-UAS Fight
summary: Counter-drone experiments in the Arizona desert are shaping how U.S. forces in the Middle East confront the drone threat.
content:
YUMA PROVING GROUND, Ariz. — For most of September, the desert here echoed with a new kind of arms race: small drones buzzing overhead, and the guns, jammers and interceptor missiles trying to knock them down.

The exercise was Falcon Peak 26.2, the fourth iteration of the counter-drone experimentation campaign and the first held at Yuma. Run by Joint Interagency Task Force 401 — the Pentagon office created in August 2025 to coordinate counter-drone efforts across the military and other agencies — it put systems from multiple vendors through scenarios modeled on the drone incursions plaguing the U.S. southern border.

## A border problem driving the testing

The numbers explain the urgency. The U.S. military detected 378 drone incursions along the U.S.-Mexico border in a single recent 30-day period. Most involve small commercial quadcopters flown by transnational cartels for reconnaissance, smuggling coordination and trafficking — cheap aircraft with tiny radar signatures that conventional air defenses struggle to track, let alone engage without risking collateral damage near populated areas.

Joint Task Force Southern Border logged nearly 400 such incursions in one 30-day stretch, officials said. The mismatch — hundred-dollar drones against million-dollar defenses — is the cost-exchange problem now defining the counter-drone fight, and the reason the Pentagon wants interceptors that cost hundreds, not hundreds of thousands, per shot.

## Permanent lanes, real conditions

Falcon Peak set up three permanent test lanes at Yuma: one for detection sensors, one for electronic defeat, one for kinetic weapons. The Army says the lanes will stay in place for ongoing testing with the Department of War, military units, industry and partners. Yuma has now been designated the primary dedicated interagency counter-small-UAS test and training range — "the blueprint" to be replicated at other ranges, in the words of one Army capability integrator.

This iteration was also the first to use Anduril's Lattice autonomous command-and-control software as the baseline for evaluating commercial sensor-to-shooter capabilities — the first deployment of Lattice for test and evaluation. Vendors ran their systems through multiple realistic scenarios in desert heat, dust, wind and glare, the conditions that make Yuma a stand-in for the border's physical challenges.

Among the systems photographed in action: Allen Control Systems' Bullfrog robotic gun turret firing at drone targets on Sept. 9, and Perseus Defense's Harpe interceptor — a 61 cm missile with a stated 2 km engagement range, launched from a portable launcher weighing under 36 kg — evaluated as a lower-cost kinetic option for use where collateral-damage constraints rule out conventional air-defense weapons.

The exercise drew the Army's top leadership, with Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle visiting for Distinguished Visitors Day on Sept. 24.

## The layered answer

Separately, JIATF-401 validated CACI's SkyValor counter-drone system for joint-force use after a June evaluation at Marine Corps Air Station Yuma, with officials calling non-kinetic defeat a crucial layer of border defense.

The lesson from Yuma is blunt: detection comes first — small drones fly low and slow with limited signatures — and no single system solves the problem. The layered answer taking shape is persistent sensors to build the air picture, electronic warfare to jam or take over the threat, and cheap kinetic interceptors for what gets through, all tested in dust and heat until they work.

title: New Leaders, New Drone Command: What to Expect from AUSA 2026
summary: The Army's autonomy push and the fate of its modernization programs will dominate this year's AUSA conference, with new leaders and a new drone command in the spotlight.
content:
WASHINGTON — The Association of the U.S. Army opens its 2026 annual meeting on Oct. 12 with the service at an inflection point: new leaders at the top, a sweeping push into autonomy and drones, and hard questions about which modernization programs survive.

The three-day gathering at the Walter E. Washington Convention Center, running Oct. 12-14, is one of North America's largest land-power events — more than 750 exhibits and tens of thousands of attendees, from Army leadership and international delegations to defense contractors and startups.

## Autonomy everywhere

Autonomous and uncrewed systems will be the most visible thread running through the conference. Tuesday's program includes sessions examining the distinction between launched effects and loitering munitions, the integration of autonomy into warfighting, and cooperation with allied partners on uncrewed and counter-uncrewed aircraft systems. Wednesday continues with aviation manned-unmanned teaming and launched effects.

The networks tying it all together get equal billing: data-centric multidomain operations, scaling command and control for the joint fight, interoperability, and an Army C2 acquisition blueprint aimed at accelerating readiness. One session, Project Flytrap, examines a data-centric "kill web" for offensive maneuver — moving information among sensors, commanders and weapons faster than the enemy can react.

After watching drones reshape the war in Ukraine, the Army is reorganizing how it buys, fields and fights with uncrewed systems. The service's autonomy push — from small quadcopters to launched effects fired from helicopters — will dominate both the formal program and the exhibit floor.

## Industry's showcase

AM General will display a redesigned next-generation HUMVEE with a 250-horsepower common-rail diesel engine, a fully autonomous unmanned ground vehicle carrying XTEND's NEST aerial-drone launch pod — letting the vehicle push a drone launch point closer to the fight without putting soldiers at risk — and the JLTV A2 fitted with Rafael drone and counter-drone technology.

Performance Drone Works, the Huntsville drone maker, will hold meetings on mission-autonomy software with Booz Allen that the company says can cut fleet software update cycles from weeks or months to hours, built for operations in denied and degraded connectivity.

Artificial intelligence and cyber operations round out the technology agenda, including a Monday session on AI-enabled cyber defense and critical-infrastructure resilience.

## The budget shadow

Under the technology buzz runs a harder conversation. With budgets under pressure and priorities shifting toward drones, long-range fires and air defense, some legacy modernization efforts face scrutiny from the new leadership.

AUSA is where the Army signals, often bluntly, what it wants to buy — and what it no longer wants. Expect contract announcements, prototype unveilings, and carefully worded warnings to programs falling behind. The conference runs through Oct. 14.

## What to watch

Watch for the Army to use AUSA as a forcing function. The service has a habit of making its priorities unmistakable on this stage — last year's themes became this year's budget lines. Programs tied to long-range precision fires, air and missile defense, and contested logistics are expected to draw the friendliest crowds; legacy efforts that cannot show relevance to the drone-saturated battlefield may hear the blunt version.

Directed energy also bears watching. After years of prototypes, the Army's laser and high-power microwave programs are approaching the point where the question shifts from whether the physics works to whether the systems can be fielded, powered and sustained. Any movement there would signal the counter-drone mission maturing from experiments like Falcon Peak into programs of record.

And underneath it all, the personnel story: new leaders means new staff, new priorities and new tolerance for risk. The officers who take the stage in mid-October will be the ones writing requirements for the next decade.

title: USCYBERCOM Wraps 13th Annual Cyber Flag Exercise with Global Partners
summary: U.S. Cyber Command has concluded its 13th annual Cyber Flag exercise after nearly three weeks of simulated cyber combat alongside global partners.
content:
SUFFOLK, Va. — U.S. Cyber Command has concluded its 13th annual Cyber Flag exercise, wrapping nearly three weeks of simulated cyber combat alongside partners and allies from around the world.

The exercise ended July 31, 2026, according to U.S. Cyber Command public affairs. More than 600 personnel from over 20 nations took part, working through simulated malicious cyber threats in a shared digital training environment built to develop a common approach to defending military networks.

## A coalition exercise

Cyber Flag has grown into the premier training event for the U.S. cyber mission force, drawing operators from across the military services and allied nations. This year's iteration closed alongside the command's 6th annual Multi-National Symposium, held July 30-31 and attended by senior officers from more than 20 countries for in-depth discussions on the issues facing an expanding cyber domain.

Army Gen. Josh Rudd — who commands U.S. Cyber Command while also serving as director of the National Security Agency and chief of the Central Security Service — addressed the symposium, stressing that multinational training and preparation are what keep nations ahead of adversaries in pace and capability.

"We never fight as a single service," Rudd said. "As a community, as a nation, as a world, we've never fought alone."

## Why it matters

The training mirrors a daily reality. State-linked hackers probe U.S. and allied military networks constantly, hunting for footholds in everything from weapons systems to logistics networks. Cyber Flag is where defenders rehearse the coordination those attacks demand — across services, agencies and national borders — before a real crisis forces it.

The exercise's scenarios test teams under realistic, high-pressure conditions: defending networks while attacks unfold, sharing threat information across organizational and classification boundaries, and making decisions at the speed the domain requires. As the Pentagon treats cyberspace as a warfighting domain alongside land, sea, air and space, exercises like this one are where the cyber mission force builds the muscle memory for coalition operations.

Cyber Command has not released details of this year's scenarios, citing operational security. What it emphasizes instead is the relationship-building. As Rudd put it, trust is not established during times of crisis — it is built in exercises like Cyber Flag, long before it is needed.

## The coalition dimension

What distinguishes Cyber Flag from a national training event is the coalition at its core. More than 20 nations sent personnel this year — operators who may one day have to defend shared networks together, under different national authorities and classification regimes. The exercise's digital terrain gives them a place to work through those frictions with simulated attacks rather than real ones.

The Multi-National Symposium alongside it serves the relationship layer: senior cyber leaders comparing notes on threats, authorities and the legal thickets of operating in a domain where the front line runs through civilian infrastructure. Those relationships are the point. When a real incident crosses borders — as major cyber incidents inevitably do — the defenders will already know the people on the other end of the secure line.

Cyber Flag is USCYBERCOM's flagship exercise, and its steady growth mirrors the command's own: cyberspace is now treated as a warfighting domain in its own right, and the cyber mission force built to fight in it keeps expanding its bench of trained operators.

title: Zero Trust Gets Harder as Every Weapon and AI Agent Needs an Identity
summary: The Pentagon's Zero Trust push is entering a harder phase: giving every user, device, weapon system, and AI agent its own verifiable identity.
content:
WASHINGTON — The Pentagon's Zero Trust cybersecurity drive is entering its hardest phase: pushing identity-based security beyond people and laptops to every weapon system, sensor and AI agent on the network.

Zero Trust assumes no user or device is trustworthy by default, verifying every access request under the principles of "never trust, always verify" and "assume breach." Extending that to weapons is a different order of difficulty. A fighter jet, a missile battery or an AI targeting assistant cannot simply be issued a password — their identities must be baked into hardware and software, resilient to jamming, spoofing and capture.

## From IT to weapons

The original 2022 Defense Department Zero Trust Strategy focused on IT infrastructure, setting 91 cybersecurity capability outcomes that all components must meet to reach target-level Zero Trust by the end of fiscal 2027, with 61 advanced-level outcomes due by fiscal 2032.

The follow-on strategy, expected around March 2026 according to Randy Resnick, senior adviser for the Pentagon's Zero Trust Portfolio Management Office, extends the mandates for the first time to operational technology, internet-of-things systems, defense critical infrastructure and weapons systems: 84 target-level outcomes due by fiscal 2030, plus 21 advanced outcomes by fiscal 2033.

A Zero Trust Implementation Guideline primer published by the department in January 2026 reinforced the approach: continuous authentication and authorization of every user, device and application, rather than reliance on perimeter defenses.

## Why weapons are harder

Operational technology presents challenges that IT-based Zero Trust was never built for. As Resnick has explained, the critical systems controlling water, power and weapons cannot simply be shut down because they are under attack — and legacy operational technology often runs on implicit trust, where security implementations must never override essential safety functions.

The stakes rise as the military networks more of its arsenal together. A single compromised node in a connected force could poison targeting data or blind commanders — exactly what adversaries are trying to achieve.

## AI agents join the identity problem

The identity challenge now extends to software. The Army's cyber command has set up a task force to build agentic cyber tools — AI agents that respond to network threats at machine speed — under an effort that includes a master kill switch to halt autonomous actions within seconds, auditable confidence thresholds and an "undo" function for agent-triggered commands, DefenseScoop reported. If agents roam the network with vulnerabilities, one officer warned, adversaries attacking the agents leaves the force exposed.

Analysts argue organizations should treat AI agents like any other non-human identity, subject to micro-segmentation and continuous monitoring.

Officials describe the identity problem as one of the pacing challenges for the Pentagon's broader digital modernization — the unglamorous work that determines whether the connected force of the 2030s can actually be trusted.

## The implementation grind

Policy is the easy part. The grind is implementation: legacy weapons and industrial systems were built for reliability and safety, not for continuous authentication, and retrofitting identity into them without breaking safety functions is painstaking work. The Navy's planned Block 2 advanced Zero Trust implementation is being watched as an early pilot for how far the model can be pushed into operational environments.

The cultural shift matters as much as the technology. "Assume breach" means designing systems that keep fighting while compromised — segmenting networks so an intruder who gets in cannot move freely, and monitoring behavior continuously so anomalies surface before damage spreads. For a force built on perimeter thinking, that is a genuine rewiring.

title: Navy Commissions Destroyer USS Ted Stevens in Alaska Ceremony
summary: The Navy has commissioned its newest destroyer, USS Ted Stevens, into active service during a ceremony in Whittier, Alaska.
content:
WHITTIER, Alaska — The U.S. Navy placed its newest guided-missile destroyer, USS Ted Stevens (DDG 128), into active commission on Oct. 3 during a formal ceremony in this deep-water port — an unusual setting that honored both the ship's namesake and Alaska's strategic weight.

The Ted Stevens is the second Flight III Arleigh Burke-class destroyer to enter service, after USS Jack H. Lucas in 2023. Its combat power centers on the Raytheon AN/SPY-6(V)1 Air and Missile Defense Radar — a 3D active electronically scanned array far more sensitive than earlier radars — paired with Lockheed Martin's Aegis Baseline 10 combat system.

## Built for missile defense

The Flight III hull is redesigned around the radar's appetite for power and cooling: three 4,000 kW gas turbine generators and upgraded air-conditioning plants feed the array. The Navy says the upgrade lets the destroyer handle anti-air warfare and ballistic missile defense simultaneously, alongside anti-submarine, anti-surface and strike missions through the Mk 41 vertical launching system.

Demand for missile-defense-capable destroyers continues to outstrip supply among the fleet's combatant commanders.

## From Pascagoula to Alaska

Huntington Ingalls Industries' Ingalls Shipbuilding division built the ship in Pascagoula, Mississippi. The keel was laid March 9, 2022; the ship launched Aug. 15, 2023; and the Navy accepted delivery on Dec. 29, 2025. She departed the yard May 8, 2026, reached Norfolk a week later, then sailed via the Panama Canal to Alaska for commissioning.

After post-commissioning operations, the destroyer will return to her homeport at Naval Station Norfolk, Virginia, joining the Atlantic Fleet.

## The namesake

The ship honors the late Sen. Ted Stevens, who represented Alaska from December 1968 to January 2009. Before politics, he flew C-46 and C-47 transport missions over "The Hump" in the China-Burma-India theater as an Army Air Forces pilot in World War II, earning the Distinguished Flying Cross. He later championed Alaska statehood and, in the Senate, defense spending, Arctic security and military pay and benefits.

Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao delivered the principal address. The ship's commanding officer, Capt. Mary Katey Hayes, told the crew they were ready to answer the nation's call. The motto: "Lead with Courage." In keeping with tradition, the sponsors — Stevens' wife Catherine Ann Stevens and daughters Susan Stevens Covich and Lily Stevens Becker — gave the order to "man our ship and bring her to life."

The Navy noted the Tlingit phrase "Woosh-Jee-een" — "working together" — as the spirit of the partnership among the Navy, the Stevens family, the crew and Alaska. Staging the ceremony in Alaska was itself a statement: the Arctic is becoming a zone of strategic competition, and the commissioning put one of the fleet's most advanced ships on display in the region's waters.

## More Flight IIIs coming

The Ted Stevens will not be the last. Five more Flight III destroyers are under construction at Ingalls Shipbuilding, according to the yard — the hulls that will carry the SPY-6 radar and Aegis Baseline 10 into the fleet through the rest of the decade. The Flight III line is, in effect, the surface Navy's air-and-missile-defense backbone for the 2030s, the ships combatant commanders will request by name when ballistic missile threats flare.

Each hull also refines the design. The power and cooling margins built into Flight III leave room for future directed-energy weapons — the Navy's long-term bet for defeating the missile salvos that could exhaust even deep magazines.
imageAlt: Navy Commissions Destroyer USS Ted Stevens in Alaska Ceremony
author: Robert Hayes

title: Air Force Names Its New Drone Wingmen: FQ-42 Vengeance and FQ-44 Fury
summary: The Air Force has officially named its first Collaborative Combat Aircraft the FQ-42 Vengeance and FQ-44 Fury.
content:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. — The Air Force has given names to its future drone wingmen. The service's first two Collaborative Combat Aircraft will be called the FQ-42A Vengeance and the FQ-44A Fury, Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink announced Sept. 14 during his keynote at the Air & Space Forces Association's Air, Space & Cyber Conference.

The naming is more than ceremony. It marks the CCA program's passage from concept to real hardware with real designations — and Meink paired it with a production target: at least 500 autonomous aircraft in service by 2032, on the way to a planned fleet of about 1,000.

"By then, our special operators will have the ability to employ thousands of autonomous one-way attack systems, and we will have autonomous fighters like the Collaborative Combat Aircraft," Meink said. "They'll perform many of the missions that manned fighters currently execute."

## Two vendors, two aircraft

General Atomics Aeronautical Systems builds the FQ-42A; Anduril Industries builds the FQ-44A. The "FQ" prefix follows Air Force convention — F for fighter, Q for unmanned. The Fury name was already in use inside Anduril; for the FQ-42, the service replaced General Atomics' internal "Dark Merlin" with Vengeance.

The aircraft moved fast. General Atomics' FQ-42A flew for the first time in August 2025, less than 18 months after contract award — "almost unheard of in aircraft development," Meink said. Anduril rolled its first FQ-44A off the assembly line in July 2026 after flight testing that began in October 2025.

In June 2026 the Air Force awarded both companies engineering, manufacturing development and production contracts for Increment 1 — ahead of schedule, after judging both designs ready for full-scale manufacturing. The service requested nearly $1 billion in fiscal 2027 funding to begin procurement, aiming for more than 150 combat-capable aircraft by the end of the decade.

## Tested in combat-relevant missions

The program has already shot live weapons. The Air Force recently completed its first live-fire test with Anduril's FQ-44A: an end-to-end, beyond-line-of-sight strike against a simulated target using an inert AIM-120 missile.

CCAs are designed as affordable, semi-autonomous unmanned aircraft that extend the reach of crewed fighters like the F-35 and the future F-47. They can carry sensors and weapons deep into contested airspace, scout ahead, jam enemy radars or strike targets — with onboard systems handling flight functions while human operators keep the higher-level mission decisions.

The service is already preparing Increment 2, expected to fold in lessons from the first aircraft and expand capabilities — the next step in a program meant to number in the thousands.

## What comes next

Increment 1 is only the opening bid. The Air Force is already preparing Increment 2, expected to widen the competition and fold in lessons from the first aircraft — more capability, possibly more vendors, and a design space that keeps evolving as autonomy software matures faster than airframes.

The CCAs are one piece of a larger family: the crewed sixth-generation F-47 now in development, the B-21 Raider, and a spreading inventory of autonomous systems from attritable one-way attack drones to long-endurance reconnaissance platforms. The vision Meink laid out is a force where crewed aircraft command swarms of uncrewed teammates — and where the service's combat mass comes increasingly from machines without pilots.
imageAlt: Air Force Names Its New Drone Wingmen: FQ-42 Vengeance and FQ-44 Fury
author: James Carter

title: NORAD F-16s Deploy to the High North for Operation Arctic Vanguard
summary: F-16s from Eielson Air Force Base have deployed to Goose Bay, Canada, for Arctic defense missions under Operation Arctic Vanguard.
content:
F-16 Fighting Falcons from Eielson Air Force Base, Alaska, have deployed to Goose Bay in Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada, to fly defense missions across the Arctic under Operation Arctic Vanguard 26-4.2.

The operation, running Sept. 13-26, pairs the Alaskan NORAD Region directly with the Canadian NORAD Region to execute what the command calls critical defense missions across the Arctic — the northern approaches an adversary's long-range bombers and cruise missiles would use against North America.

## Beyond Goose Bay

The deployment does not stop in Canada. NORAD personnel and aircraft are to forward deploy into Greenland for operations in austere conditions alongside partners from Denmark and other NATO countries — staging combat airpower from Alaska, through northeastern Canada, to the Greenland ice cap in a single operational sequence.

"Operation Arctic Vanguard demonstrates that austere conditions and vast distances present no barrier to NORAD's collective defense," said Air Force Lt. Gen. Robert D. Davis, commander of the Alaskan NORAD Region. "Deploying combat airpower from Alaska across Canada and forward into Greenland validates our agile combat capabilities."

The operation supports the NORAD and U.S. Northern Command "Nordic Bridge" concept, which aligns the commands' Arctic operations, exercises, training and investments with NATO and regional partners.

## Agile combat, Arctic conditions

The move is a practical test of agile combat employment: can multi-role fighters be shifted rapidly from the Pacific theater, sustained across vast distances, and generated for air-superiority missions in sub-zero, infrastructure-poor environments? Royal Canadian Air Force strategic airlift — including CC-177 Globemaster IIIs loading 354th Fighter Wing cargo at Eielson — supported the deployment, and a KC-135 Stratotanker flew in formation with the F-16s over Greenland on Sept. 16.

The Eielson jets are no strangers to extreme cold, routinely training in Arctic conditions. Operating from Goose Bay extends their reach over the North Atlantic and eastern Arctic.

## Why the High North matters

The Arctic has become a growing security concern. Russia has reopened Cold War-era bases along its northern coast; China calls itself a "near-Arctic state" and keeps expanding its icebreaker fleet. NORAD, the joint U.S.-Canadian command, owns the mission of detecting and intercepting threats across the region.

Arctic Vanguard is part of a recurring series of NORAD and Northern Command operations meant to build presence, practice operating from forward Arctic locations and defend the continent's northern approaches. NORAD has not disclosed how many aircraft are involved or the exact Greenland operating location.

## A familiar mission, a harder neighborhood

NORAD's Arctic watch is not new — the command has intercepted Russian long-range aircraft near Alaska for decades, and the F-16s at Eielson sit alert for exactly that mission. What is new is the tempo and the company: operations like Arctic Vanguard now routinely fold in allies, push into Greenland, and rehearse the logistics of sustaining fighters where there is little infrastructure and less margin for error.

The geography tells the story. From Eielson to Goose Bay to Greenland runs the corridor any northern attack would travel — and the corridor any northern defense must hold. Each iteration of Arctic Vanguard makes that corridor a little more practiced, a little less theoretical.
imageAlt: NORAD F-16s Deploy to the High North for Operation Arctic Vanguard
author: Michael Reynolds

title: B-52 to Get Stealthy LRASM Anti-Ship Missiles, Completing the Bomber Trio
summary: The B-52 is being integrated with the stealthy AGM-158C LRASM, giving all three U.S. bombers a long-range anti-ship punch.
content:
The B-52 Stratofortress is in line for the AGM-158C Long Range Anti-Ship Missile, after Naval Air Systems Command announced Oct. 7 that it intends to award Lockheed Martin a sole-source contract to integrate the stealthy weapon onto the Air Force's oldest bomber.

The planned cost-plus-fixed-fee delivery order covers LRASM integration on the B-52, including missile software updates, associated testing, repair of test assets and failure review boards. The notice gives no schedule for completing the integration or fielding the capability.

## An arsenal plane for maritime strike

The B-52 can already carry up to 20 AGM-158 Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missiles — the family LRASM is derived from, sharing similar dimensions — and the notice does not specify how many LRASMs the bomber would ultimately carry. The idea has circulated since at least 2019, when Naval News first reported the possibility, but languished for years until the current push.

Retired Air Force Col. Mark Gunzinger, a former B-52 pilot now with the Mitchell Institute, told Air & Space Forces Magazine that "a handful of B-52s will be able to deliver more weapons on maritime targets and do so over much longer ranges than the Navy's carrier-based aircraft per day."

## The missile

LRASM is a subsonic, stealthy cruise missile built by Lockheed Martin as a variant of the AGM-158B JASSM-ER. It flies more than 200 nautical miles, using radio-frequency and infrared seekers plus a datalink to find and identify ships autonomously — including when GPS is jammed and datalinks are denied, the conditions expected in a Pacific fight.

The AGM-158C-3 variant, expected to be procured for the first time this fiscal year, adds improved beyond-line-of-sight targeting, better electronic counter-countermeasures and software upgrades.

## Spreading across the force

The B-1B already carries LRASM, and the Air Force revealed earlier this year that the stealthy B-2 can launch it as well — a capability not previously disclosed. Navy F/A-18E/F Super Hornets fly it today; integration is underway for the F-15, the Marine Corps and Navy F-35 variants and the P-8A Poseidon, and the future B-21 is certain to follow.

The move reflects the Pentagon's focus on the Indo-Pacific, where China's navy — now the world's largest by hull count — is the pacing challenge. Holding that fleet at risk from long range, from multiple launch axes, is a central element of U.S. war planning.

## A widening family of launchers

The B-52 is one node in a widening LRASM launch network. Integration work continues for the F-15, the Marine Corps and Navy F-35 variants and the P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft — the Navy has already shown a P-8A carrying the missile in flight — and a surface-launch variant has been trialed. Each new platform multiplies the axes a defender must watch.

The AGM-158C-3, the newest variant expected to enter procurement this fiscal year, pushes the missile further into GPS-denied, heavily jammed environments with better beyond-line-of-sight targeting. The trajectory is clear: more launchers, smarter seekers, longer reach — a distributed maritime strike architecture built for a theater as vast as the Pacific.

title: U.S. Pitches F-35 as Portugal Weighs Replacing Its F-16s
summary: Washington is making a hard push for the F-35 as Portugal decides what will replace its aging F-16 fleet.
content:
LISBON — The United States is pressing Portugal to choose the F-35 for its next fighter, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio promising Lisbon a "very competitive" American offer during an Oct. 8 visit.

Portuguese Foreign Minister Paulo Rangel, standing alongside Rubio, said the government is seriously considering the F-35A Lightning II — along with the Eurofighter Typhoon, Dassault Rafale and Saab Gripen E — to replace the air force's aging F-16s.

"The Portuguese state will always decide in accordance with the national interest," Rangel said at the news conference. "There is one point that is also clear: we are seriously considering the F-35 proposal, just as we are considering others."

## A 5 billion euro decision

The requirement covers Portugal's fleet of upgraded F-16M fighters — 28 by some counts — with a possible buy of 27 to 28 aircraft valued near 5 billion euros, one of Lisbon's largest planned military investments. The War Zone reports the current operational fleet as 25 modernized F-16AM/BMs — 21 single-seat and four two-seat aircraft — based at Monte Real Air Base.

Portugal acquired 45 F-16A/B Block 15 aircraft through the Peace Atlantis I and II programs, with the first new-build jets delivered from 1994 to equip Esquadra 201 "Falcoes." Whatever Lisbon picks next will anchor its airpower for decades.

## A reopened door

The American push follows a cold spell. In March 2025, Portugal questioned the reliability of long-term U.S. defense commitments — citing "allied predictability" as a fundamental asset — and shelved F-35 plans in favor of European options. The Oct. 8 meeting reopened the prospect of a major American fighter sale.

Competition is already formal. Dassault Aviation submitted a Rafale offer to the Portuguese government and air force in July 2026, then signed a cooperation protocol with the AED Cluster Portugal industry association on Sept. 23 alongside Thales and Safran. Lockheed Martin signed a similar protocol with the same association in June 2025; the Eurofighter consortium and Saab have followed on identical, non-exclusive terms.

## No tender yet

Lisbon has not formally launched a replacement competition. The chief of the defense staff, Gen. Joao Cartaxo Alves — who as air force commander favored the F-35A — has said the F-16 replacement will be written into a new military programming law still to go to parliament; a tender can follow only after adoption, unless the government chooses a government-to-government deal.

For Washington, the stakes go beyond one sale: keeping a NATO ally inside the F-35 ecosystem preserves interoperability, training pipelines and industrial ties for decades. For Lisbon, the choice balances capability, cost and strategic alignment — and, as Rangel made clear, will be decided on national interest.

## The industrial contest

The competition is being fought as much in factories as in the skies. All four contenders have signed cooperation protocols with AED Cluster Portugal, the domestic aerospace association — Lockheed Martin in June 2025, Dassault (with Thales and Safran) in September 2026, the Eurofighter consortium and Saab on the same non-exclusive terms. Each is promising Portuguese industry a share of production, maintenance and future technology.

The F-35's industrial pitch rests on scale: the program's global supply chain and a European operator base that keeps growing, which spreads sustainment costs and guarantees decades of upgrade work. The Europeans counter with promises of deeper local workshare and fewer political strings. Lisbon's decision will reveal which argument a mid-size NATO air force finds more persuasive.
