author: David Sullivan

title: Germany Finally Gives Its F125 Frigates Real Teeth with IRIS-T Missiles
summary: Germany is arming its 7,200-ton F125 frigates with IRIS-T SLM surface-to-air missiles, addressing their notoriously light armament.
content:
Germany is finally giving its biggest warships real air defenses. On Oct. 2, 2026, Diehl Defence and the federal procurement office BAAINBw signed an adaptation development contract to fit the naval version of the IRIS-T SLM surface-to-air missile to the German Navy's four F125 frigates — nine days after the Bundestag's budget committee approved the program on Sept. 23.

Each 7,200-ton frigate will receive two deck-mounted launchers holding 16 missiles apiece: 32 interceptors per ship, in vertical-launch canisters, against aircraft, helicopters, cruise missiles, and drones. The missile reaches 40 kilometers out and 20 kilometers up, guided by datalink with terminal self-homing.

The four ships of the Baden-Württemberg class — Baden-Württemberg, Nordrhein-Westfalen, Sachsen-Anhalt, Rheinland-Pfalz — were built for stabilization and crisis-management missions, and their armament showed it: short-range anti-ship missiles and two RIM-116 RAM point-defense launchers on a hull the size of a destroyer. The gap became a public embarrassment in 2024, when Baden-Württemberg detoured around Africa rather than transit the Red Sea on its return from an Indo-Pacific deployment.

## From concept to firing in ten months

The program is moving fast because the hard part is already done. In October 2025, during a naval firing exercise off Norway, engineers bolted a demonstrator launcher to the C-deck of Baden-Württemberg and engaged multiple targets using the ship's own radar data — going from concept to live firing in under ten months.

The naval adaptation strips out the ground system's support legs and hydraulics to save weight and deck space. Functional prototypes are expected in 2027, with sea trials and the first operational test launches the same year.


Diehl's own description of the goal is deliberately modest: "The aim is to make the system mission-capable on the German Navy's F125 frigates." But the engineering is not trivial. The naval IRIS-T SLM drops the ground launcher's support legs and hydraulics, fires from a compact vertical canister, and stays in contact with the ship via datalink until its own seeker takes over for the terminal phase — a fire-and-update architecture built for saturation attacks by drones and sea-skimmers.

## A missile with a combat record

The IRIS-T SLM is not a paper missile. German-supplied batteries in Ukraine have intercepted Shahed drones and Kh-101 and Kalibr cruise missiles at ranges up to 40 kilometers, and Berlin has explicitly cited that operational record in justifying the frigate upgrade.

The move fits Germany's broader post-2022 naval rearmament — new F126 frigates and Type 212CD submarines with Norway are in the pipeline alongside missile upgrades across the fleet. But the F125 fix is the most symbolically loaded: the ships were designed in an era when Berlin assumed its navy would police crises, not fight wars.

For a navy that watched its F124 frigate Hessen swat Houthi drones over the Red Sea under the EU's Operation Aspides while its newest, largest frigates lacked comparable defenses, the contract closes what The War Zone called one of the most conspicuous weaknesses in a Western fleet. Thirty-two missiles per ship will not make the F125 an air-defense destroyer. But it will, at last, give it teeth.

title: South Korea Tests First Homegrown Hypersonic Glide Vehicle
summary: South Korea conducted its first successful flight test of a domestically developed hypersonic boost-glide vehicle on Oct. 8, with President Lee Jae Myung observing, marking the country's entry into a hypersonic arms race on the Korean Peninsula.
content:
South Korea has carried out the first successful flight test of a domestically developed hypersonic boost-glide vehicle, which its president says gives the country a new strategic strike option against critical targets on the Korean Peninsula.

The test took place on Oct. 8 at the Anheung Proving Ground on the country's western coast and was observed in person by President Lee Jae Myung, Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul and other officials, according to a Korean-language announcement from the presidential office, the Cheong Wa Dae, released the following day.

The Agency for Defense Development, which manages the range, launched the weapon from a wheeled transporter-erector-launcher mounted on a platform just off the coast. After the booster carried the glide vehicle to its target altitude, the vehicle separated, descended to a lower altitude and flew a planned course that included irregular vertical and horizontal maneuvers before striking a designated sea target, the release said.

The flight verified core technologies — ultra-high-temperature heat-resistant materials, guidance and control, and irregular maneuvering at low altitudes under hypersonic conditions. The announcement described the system as a key strategic asset able to launch surprise precision strikes on critical targets during a crisis, thanks to an unpredictable flight path and extreme speed.

No formal name for the missile has been disclosed, and the government did not say how far the vehicle traveled or how fast it flew.

## A first look at the design

Stills released by the presidential office show the missile leaving its launcher and the glider impacting the water at the end of its flight, captured from the air by what appears to be an electro-optical camera. The War Zone's analysis of the low-resolution images found a broadly conical body with stabilizing fins, at least one truncated, with hints of a wedge-shaped design — though the resolution is too poor for certainty.

The same day, Lee inspected a transporter-erector-launcher for the Hyunmoo-5, the country's newest and heaviest ballistic missile, which entered service around the end of last year. The 35-ton missile is officially classed as short-range, a classification attributed largely to its 17,000-pound warhead, already a threat to deeply buried North Korean facilities. The government has not drawn an explicit connection between the Hyunmoo-5 and the glide-vehicle test, and South Korea is separately developing an air-breathing hypersonic cruise missile along with new air- and sea-launched ballistic missiles.

## A sharpening contest on the peninsula

The test came days after North Korea announced its leader had overseen a test of an intermediate-range hypersonic missile, the second purported hypersonic launch by Pyongyang in recent weeks. It also followed a Sept. 21 incident along the Demilitarized Zone in which three South Korean troops were wounded by what Seoul says was a North Korean landmine — a charge Pyongyang denies and warned would draw a powerful counteraction if Seoul retaliated.

Seoul says its missile-defense network could still detect and intercept the North's new weapons. But the exchange underscores a contest both sides now describe in hypersonic terms.

## Why it matters

One successful test does not make an arsenal. Hypersonic boost-glide vehicles are among the hardest weapons in the world to field: guidance through the mid-course and terminal phases — the hardest technical problems — was not demonstrated by this flight, and years typically separate first tests from operational deployment.

But the signal is deliberate. Seoul is moving toward deterrence by credible reach against the North's leadership bunkers and mobile launchers, the core of its Korea Massive Punishment and Retaliation doctrine. A maneuvering glider that flies low and fast compresses Pyongyang's already thin warning time and forces its radar network to track a target that refuses a predictable arc — a bunker-buster on top of a decapitation-strike weapon.

The audience is wider than North Korea. The test tells Washington, Beijing and Moscow that South Korea intends to master the defining strike technology of the decade rather than depend on American systems alone. The risk is the familiar one on the peninsula: every Southern advance invites a Northern reply.

title: Houthi Missile Strike on Riyadh Airport Kills 12, Wounds 309
summary: A missile struck a passenger terminal at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Oct. 10, killing at least 12 and wounding 309 in Saudi Arabia's deadliest attack in more than a decade, as President Trump said he was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis.
content:
A missile struck a passenger terminal at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Saturday, killing at least 12 people and wounding 309 in Saudi Arabia's deadliest attack in more than a decade, the kingdom's civil aviation authority said.

The strike landed late Saturday afternoon — the third missile attack this week on the airport, which serves a capital of about eight million people. The dead included four Saudis, two Bangladeshis and one national each of the United States, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine and Sudan, the authority said. The wounded, some in critical condition, were rushed to hospitals by ambulance and helicopter.

More than 600 flights were cancelled and the kingdom's second-busiest airport was closed until at least late Sunday. Schools across Riyadh moved to remote learning for a week. Video from inside the terminal showed debris strewn across a dust-filled hall.

A senior Houthi official, Nasr al-Din Amer, appeared to acknowledge responsibility, writing on X: "We shut down Riyadh international airport." The group later warned airlines and travelers to avoid Saudi airports and airspace — except those serving Mecca and Medina — saying Saudi Arabia "will bear responsibility for any failed attempts to intercept" its missiles.

## A week of attacks

Two earlier strikes on the airport this week killed four people and heavily damaged a Saudi commercial aircraft. A Thursday attack destroyed a passenger jet on the tarmac and killed three people, including a pilot, prompting Britain to advise against all but essential travel to Riyadh. Several airlines, including Lufthansa and Emirates, cancelled flights to the capital, and the United States, Britain, Spain and Canada warned their citizens against using the airport.

The Saudi-led coalition's spokesman, Turki al-Malki, called Saturday's attack a war crime against a civilian facility and said the joint forces command would respond firmly within the bounds of international law. The UN's special envoy for Yemen, Hans Grundberg, called the attacks a grave escalation, and the secretary-general condemned strikes on civilian infrastructure as violations of international law.

## Trump weighs joining Saudi strikes

President Donald Trump said he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis in Yemen — a step he had previously resisted. "We may. We're going to look at it," he told reporters, adding that he planned to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Last month, Trump rejected two Saudi appeals for direct American strikes, CNN reported at the time.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed an American citizen was among the dead and condemned the attack as showing a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life.

The Houthi campaign is the sharp end of a Yemen war that flared up again this summer after years of relative calm. The group began striking Saudi infrastructure, including oil refineries, after announcing in July it would target Saudi shipping in the Red Sea in retaliation for a Saudi blockade on the capital Sanaa. Last month, Houthi forces captured the port of Mocha and closed in on Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, while a Saudi-backed government offensive struggled to retake ground.

## Why it matters

The Houthis have crossed a line they have spent years probing. They have not merely struck Saudi Arabia; they have shown they can repeatedly hit a prestige civilian target in the capital, forcing the closure of an international airport and driving airlines away. That strikes directly at the kingdom's drive to become a global business and tourism destination.

For the air-defense picture, the repeated terminal hits matter as much as the casualties. Saudi Arabia operates some of the world's densest missile-defense coverage, yet missiles are getting through, reportedly as the kingdom's interceptor stocks run low — the AP reported last month that Riyadh had sought air-defense help from France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt. It is the same demand signal driving the Pentagon's own rush to replenish stocks and field next-generation interceptors.

And Washington now faces its hardest version of the Houthi question. An American is dead, a partner's capital airport is closed, and the crown prince wants American firepower. Trump resisted twice; a third ask, after this, is much harder to refuse — and American strikes would widen a war already spreading from Yemen's Red Sea coast to Riyadh's departure gates.

title: Anduril Unveils Steelfin, a Modular Family of Affordable Interceptors for Drone, Cruise and Hypersonic Threats
summary: Anduril unveiled Steelfin, a family of two-stage surface-to-air interceptors aimed at cruise, ballistic and hypersonic missiles, pitched at a fraction of the cost of today's interceptors with production scaled to thousands of rounds a year.
content:
WASHINGTON - Anduril Industries has unveiled Steelfin, a family of configurable surface-to-air interceptors designed to defeat cruise missiles, ballistic missiles, hypersonic weapons and even low-cost attack drones - at what the company calls a fraction of the cost of current interceptors.

The company announced Steelfin on Monday at the Association of the U.S. Army's annual meeting in Washington, its first entry into a market long dominated by Lockheed Martin and Raytheon - and the latest move in an industry sprint toward cheaper interceptors built in the thousands rather than the hundreds.

Steelfin is built around a common two-stage architecture. The first stage is a swappable solid rocket booster - Anduril says it is integrating boosters of 10-inch, 18-inch and 21-inch diameters, including quad-pack and dual-pack arrangements for the Navy's Mk 41 Vertical Launch System. The second stage is a shared "terminal interceptor" carrying the same baseline airframe, avionics, software, flight controls and interfaces across the family, with hit-to-kill and blast-fragmentation options planned.

## Built to fire from what the military already owns

The main selling point is launcher compatibility: Steelfin variants are designed to fire from the M903A2 launcher used by Patriot batteries, the Navy's Mk 41 VLS, the Army's Typhon mid-range launcher and emerging containerized launchers, working with existing fire control systems like Aegis and the Army's Integrated Battle Command System. Anduril plans to build several thousand missiles a year on shared tooling so output can shift to whichever variant is in demand.

Anduril has not yet flown a Steelfin missile - it has completed ballistic testing, plans flight tests next year and targets full-rate production in late 2028 or early 2029, declining to name the customers it says co-invested in the multi-year effort.

## The cost argument

The central claim is cost: executives say one configuration should cost roughly a third of a Patriot PAC-3 MSE interceptor - about $5.3 million per round in the Army's latest budget, versus roughly $15.5 million for a THAAD interceptor and $2.5 million for the Navy's newest SM-2.

"Our military and our allies' militaries are struggling with a set of legacy interceptors that are not scalable, and are not able to match the volume of the threat that they are facing," Chris Brose, Anduril's president and chief strategy officer, told reporters ahead of the announcement.

The timing is deliberate. This month alone, Raytheon received contracts worth up to $6.3 billion for SM-3 Block IB interceptors and up to $24.4 billion for SM-6 missiles, and Lockheed Martin unveiled its PAC-3 Edge interceptor on Friday. The Army has also sought proposals for a Patriot-compatible interceptor below $1 million a round - a requirement Anduril says Steelfin is vying for, alongside the service's Future Interceptor program.

## Why it matters: the magazine problem is now a factory problem

The most important thing about Steelfin is not any single performance claim - it is the diagnosis behind the design. Combat in the Middle East and Ukraine has made the interceptor shortage structural: defenders keep spending exquisite, million-dollar missiles against cheap drones and massed salvos, and no existing production line can replace what gets fired. This month's $6.3 billion SM-3 deal and $24.4 billion SM-6 award are the Pentagon's answer so far, and both are multi-year attempts to refill magazines that combat keeps draining.

Steelfin's bet is that the bottleneck is architecture, not just money. Legacy interceptors were built as bespoke weapons, each with its own tooling, suppliers and production line, which is why output cannot surge when demand spikes. A family sharing one terminal stage and one line tries to industrialize the interceptor like a commercial platform - redirecting capacity toward whichever threat is surging.

That mirrors where the Navy itself is headed: its Naval Modular Missile initiative envisions a similar common-terminal-stage family, aiming to eventually replace the Standard Missile family. The caveats are real - Steelfin has not flown, has no named customer, and Anduril has never built a surface-to-air missile. But with Lockheed answering on cost through the PAC-3 Edge and the Pentagon writing multi-year checks to rebuild stockpiles, Anduril has planted a flag on the exact intersection of affordability and volume every service is trying to solve.

title: Airbus Flies Kratos Valkyrie Drone in Europe for the First Time, Targets 2029 Eurofighter Wingman
summary: Airbus carried out the first European test flight of the Kratos-built Valkyrie combat drone it hopes to team with Eurofighters, flying the rocket-launched aircraft to Mach 0.8 with a combat-ready wingman targeted for 2029.
content:
BERLIN - Airbus has carried out the first test flight in Europe of the U.S.-built Valkyrie combat drone it hopes to team with Eurofighter jets, a milestone in its bid to give Germany an uncrewed wingman aircraft by 2029.

The flight took place on Sept. 29 at a test site in northern Europe that the companies did not name, Airbus Defence and Space CEO Michael Schoellhorn told Reuters. The aircraft, which Airbus designates the U740 Valkyrie, launched from a rail using a rocket booster - no runway required - flew at various altitudes and speeds up to Mach 0.8, and had its mission retasked in flight.

"We tried all sorts of things and were very impressed, so it was a complete success," Schoellhorn said in an interview. He said the flight's primary significance was proving that the regulatory clearances needed to operate military drones in Europe's complex airspace can be secured.

The Valkyrie is based on the XQ-58 built by U.S.-based Kratos Defense, which has been flying in the United States since 2019. Under a partnership announced in 2025, Airbus plans to offer a combat-ready drone to the German Air Force by 2029, with the aircraft able to fly autonomously, under remote piloting or in teaming with Eurofighters. The European version is 9.1 meters long with an 8.2-meter wingspan, weighs about 3 metric tons at takeoff, has a range exceeding 5,000 kilometers, a ceiling of 45,000 feet, an internal weapons bay and pylons under its wings. The estimated unit cost is around 20 million euros.

## Flying without the European brain - for now

Notably, this first flight did not yet carry Airbus's own mission system, called MARS. The software and hardware suite is the component that will let the aircraft fly missions autonomously and coordinate groups of drones, with a human kept "on the loop" to approve critical decisions. Airbus describes MARS as the sovereign European element of the program, giving Germany and other buyers full control of the software, data and mission hardware rather than dependence on the U.S. manufacturer.

Schoellhorn said the Valkyrie is expected to fly with MARS on board for its next test flight in the first quarter of 2027, and the first flight actually teamed with a Eurofighter is scheduled for later that year. No order for the drone has been placed yet - the 2029 combat-readiness target is an offer, not a contract.

## A crowded race for loyal wingmen

Airbus is entering an increasingly crowded field. Boeing, Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, General Atomics, Anduril Industries and Saab are all building uncrewed combat aircraft aimed at what could become a multibillion-dollar global market for collaborative combat aircraft - so-called loyal wingmen.

The regulatory angle matters especially in Germany. In 2013, Berlin cancelled the Northrop-built Euro Hawk drone after a wrangle over European civil certification rules, a failure that still haunts the country's drone ambitions. Schoellhorn framed the Sept. 29 flight as proof that such barriers can be overcome this time.

## Why it matters: sovereignty is the product, the drone is the vehicle

Read past the flight and the story is really about a procurement model Europe keeps demanding: proven foreign hardware, European brains. Pairing Kratos's already-flying airframe with a European mission system Berlin fully controls is exactly what the Euro Hawk failure taught Germany to require - control of the software, data and weapons integration. The engineering risk is lower than a clean-sheet drone, but the hard part - MARS integration, Eurofighter teaming and European certification - all lies ahead. The early-2027 flight with MARS aboard will be the real milestone.

The 2029 target is aggressive, with no order placed and the teaming demonstration more than a year out. What may push Berlin is arithmetic: a wingman at roughly 20 million euros a unit offers combat mass at a fraction of a crewed fighter's cost, and Germany's air force, like every NATO air force, is short of affordable mass. If the MARS flight and the Eurofighter teaming demo hit their marks, the Valkyrie becomes a genuine procurement candidate - not just for Germany, but for every European air force adding drone mass without surrendering sovereignty over the software controlling it.

author: David Sullivan

title: Sikorsky Packs Four Nomad 100 Drones Into One Shipping Container for Rapid Combat Deployment
summary: Sikorsky unveiled the Nomad 100 Fast Pack at the Army's annual conference: a standard 20-foot container holding four VTOL combat drones and everything needed to fly them, with two aircraft mission-ready in under 15 minutes.
content:
WASHINGTON - Sikorsky has packed a small drone air force into a shipping container.

The Lockheed Martin subsidiary introduced the Nomad 100 Fast Pack on Monday, a containerized vertical-takeoff-and-landing uncrewed aircraft kit unveiled as the Association of the U.S. Army's annual conference opened in Washington. A single standard 20-foot ISO container holds four Nomad 100 drones along with the mission-command software, power, communications and sustainment equipment needed to fly them - a complete expeditionary drone detachment that fits on the back of a truck.

## Ready in minutes, no runway needed

The headline figure is speed. Sikorsky says that in its planned configuration, two of the four aircraft can be mission ready in less than 15 minutes, with the other two available within four to six hours. The system launches without a runway, from sites such as naval vessels, tactical vehicle staging areas and improvised landing zones. After a mission, crews can repack the container, load it onto a compatible vehicle and move to a new site.

Depending on how a customer configures it, the kit can run intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and targeting missions, along with light attack and contested logistics - the expeditionary ISR-T, strike and multirole portfolio the Pentagon has been urging industry to scale up.

"Military leaders are challenging industry to expand the inventory of uncrewed aircraft, and Sikorsky is delivering proven autonomous air capability with speed and scale, offering field-ready solutions to deploy and sustain those systems where they are needed most," Rich Benton, Sikorsky's vice president and general manager, said in the company's announcement.

## A proven airframe in new packaging

The aircraft inside the container is not a clean-sheet design. The Nomad 100, with an 18-foot wingspan, is a Group 3 uncrewed aircraft under Pentagon classification, built around Sikorsky's rotor-blown-wing design - helicopter-style vertical lift and hover paired with the speed, range and endurance of a fixed-wing aircraft - and flown with the company's MATRIX autonomy software. It completed initial ground and flight testing in July as part of DARPA's Evade demonstration, Aviation Week reported, and is a larger sibling of the Nomad 50, which first flew in March 2025.

Sikorsky has not disclosed the Nomad 100's payload, range or endurance, Military Times noted - a deliberate gap that keeps the focus on what the company is really selling here. It is not pitching the airframe; it is pitching the logistics wrapper.

## Why it matters

The Fast Pack is a bet that the Pentagon's drone problem is no longer about building better aircraft - it is about getting good-enough aircraft forward fast. Two years of watching uncrewed systems in Ukraine, the Red Sea and now the war with Iran have taught the U.S. military that runway-dependent drone bases are fragile and that repositioning speed matters as much as payload. A containerized kit that arrives with its own command, power and sustainment gear is designed for exactly that lesson.

The naval angle is worth watching. The system is explicitly designed to launch from ships, which makes the Fast Pack a cross-service product rather than an Army-only one - a notable hedge at a time when the services are competing for drone funding. Group 3 is also a deliberate choice: large enough to carry real ISR and light-attack payloads, small enough to deploy by the handful.

What to watch: whether the Army - or the Navy - converts the AUSA pitch into actual procurement. Sikorsky has not named a customer, a price or a delivery timeline, and containerized drone kits from other vendors have struggled to move from conference-floor concept to program of record. The next sign of traction will be a military unit or service acquisition office signing for the first kit.

title: Lockheed Unveils PAC-3 Edge, Its Bid for the Army's Future Patriot Interceptor
summary: Lockheed Martin revealed the PAC-3 Edge, a next-generation Patriot interceptor with a new seeker and rocket motor that promises longer range and higher-altitude kills at roughly the cost of the current PAC-3 MSE.
content:
WASHINGTON - Lockheed Martin has pulled the wraps off its bid to give the Army a next-generation Patriot interceptor - and its pitch is as much about the price tag as the technology.

The PAC-3 Edge, unveiled ahead of the Association of the U.S. Army's annual conference, is Lockheed's offering for the Army's Future Interceptor program, a competition to develop a follow-on to the current PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE) interceptor. Tim Cahill, president of Lockheed's missiles and fire control unit, told Breaking Defense that the company was one of two firms selected to advance in the program. He declined to name the other competitor, and the Army did not respond to a request for more information.

## New seeker, new motor

The Edge builds on the battle-tested PAC-3 MSE. Three upgrades define it: a new company-built seeker, upgraded flight controls, and a multi-pulse solid rocket motor designed by Northrop Grumman. Lockheed says the combination extends the interceptor's reach to higher altitudes and longer ranges, with better sensitivity to pick up difficult targets and better maneuverability to chase them.

"PAC-3 Edge is designed to go after the most stressing targets that we - and, more importantly, that the Department of War - believes are the next-generation threats that they are going to be seeing in the fight from our adversaries," Cahill said in an interview with Breaking Defense, referring to the Pentagon by its new secondary name.

"PAC-3 Edge will be longer ranged. It will be higher altitude. It will be more capable to take on targets that are trying to hide," he added. "It will have greater sensitivity in its seeker. It will have greater capability to maneuver and to respond to threats."

The seeker is built at Lockheed's Strigo Product Center, backed by $250 million in company investment. Cahill said $50 million to $100 million or more has already been spent on the missile, with hundreds of millions more planned, and Lockheed is displaying a full-scale model at the AUSA conference.

## A price-driven pitch

The sharpest part of the sales pitch is cost. "The cost of this would be about that of the existing PAC-3 MSE," Cahill told Reuters - roughly $4 million per missile, according to Military Times - removing the exact objection that sank the Army's last attempt at a next-generation Patriot interceptor. Army leaders scrapped that earlier effort in 2024, calling it "very expensive," Breaking Defense reported, before reviving the requirement as the Future Interceptor program.

The timeline is aggressive but framed as company-backed development rather than a Pentagon research effort: test flights targeted for 2027 and residual operational capability by 2031, goals Cahill tied to Lockheed's internal funding. At full production, Cahill told Reuters, output could reach about 2,000 missiles a year - matching the rate the Pentagon agreed in January to lift PAC-3 production toward.

## Why it matters

The PAC-3 Edge is the clearest sign yet of how the Pentagon's missile-defense buying has changed. A year ago the pattern was familiar: a new interceptor grew expensive, the Army canceled it, and the requirement died. Now the requirement is back - but only with a contractor willing to build the better missile at the same price and fund the early development itself. That is not Lockheed being generous; it is the industry reading the current Pentagon's demand for cheaper, faster, contractor-invested development.

The unveiling lands amid the biggest interceptor production wave in recent memory. Days earlier the Pentagon awarded Raytheon up to $6.3 billion to keep building SM-3 Block IB interceptors through 2034, and last month Lockheed landed a potential $20.7 billion AMRAAM deal. Across every layer, Washington is signing multiyear deals to lock in production, restock arsenals drawn down by Ukraine and Middle East conflicts, and feed the Golden Dome homeland defense initiative.

What to watch: the identity of the second Future Interceptor competitor, which will say a lot about the Army's tolerance for risk; whether the 2027 test schedule holds, since it underpins the entire company-funded model; and the funding ramp the program is slated to receive beginning in fiscal year 2028 - the moment this stops being Lockheed's pitch and becomes the Pentagon's commitment.
